title: Sent (Acts 13:1–3)
hook: while they fast and pray, Barnabas and Saul are set apart

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rhoda at the gate, so glad she left Peter knocking. Your line was she forgot to open.

Three verses. That's all Luke spends on the moment that starts the great journeys of Paul, the ones that carried the gospel across the Mediterranean. No vision on a road this time, no earthquake, no angel. Just a church in Antioch doing something ordinary: worshiping, and going without food.
screen: `THREE VERSES.` → `NO VISION THIS TIME.` → `AN ORDINARY CHURCH IN ANTIOCH.`

segments.voice: Luke bothers to list the names. In the church at Antioch there are prophets and teachers: Barnabas. Simeon, who was called Niger, a Latin nickname meaning dark or black. Lucius of Cyrene, from North Africa. Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, the same Herod who killed John the Baptist. And Saul, the former persecutor. A Cypriot, likely an African or two, a man raised in a royal court, and a converted enemy: that's the leadership. As they minister to the Lord and fast, the Holy Spirit speaks, paraphrased here: set apart for me Barnabas and Saul, for the work to which I have called them. The Greek word for set apart means to mark off, to separate for a purpose. Paul later begins his letter to the Romans calling himself separated for the gospel of God, the same root. And the church doesn't send them off at once. It fasts and prays again. Then they lay their hands on the two men, and send them away. The church let go of two of its five best teachers. Sending costs something. Catholics see a pattern here that the Church still follows: prayer and fasting before big decisions, and the laying on of hands to mark someone sent for a task, as in ordination today. And notice who speaks first in this story: not a committee, but the Spirit, heard by people who had made a little quiet by going without.
screen: `FIVE NAMES, MANY PLACES.` · `MINISTERING AND FASTING.` · `SET APART FOR THE WORK.` · `HANDS LAID ON, AND SENT.` · then, large: `SET APART.`

segments.voice: Picture one small thing you could go without, the phone at meals, the second coffee, the background noise in the car, and the gap it would leave; that gap is the kind of room the church in Antioch prayed in. In the quiet you have right now, ask what you might be set apart for: not a mission across the sea, maybe a person, a task, a conversation. If you pray, offer that small fast and simply listen.
Sent. Barnabas and Saul, set apart while the church fasted and prayed, given the laying on of hands, and let go. Today's word.
Your line: set apart. Tomorrow, a hard question, and a council to settle it. See you there.

howItsDone: Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday and abstain from meat on Lenten Fridays, many add small fasts of their own, and in ordination the bishop lays his hands on the one being ordained in silence.

original.note: Greek: set apart, mark off for a purpose. the root behind Paul calling himself separated for the gospel.

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul decided to become a missionary.
what it means: a fasting, praying church hears the Spirit, and gives up two of its own teachers for the work.
what a scholar hears: the leaders' names point to Cyprus, Cyrene and Herod's court. the verb for set apart is the same root Paul uses of himself in Romans 1:1.

chat.says: How did Paul's big journeys start? Did he just decide to go one day?
options: As Antioch's church fasted, the Spirit said set them apart; they prayed and sent him off.
An angel freed him from prison and told him to sail across the sea that night.
The apostles in Jerusalem voted to send him, since he spoke the best Greek.
chat.meaning: As the church at Antioch ministered and fasted, the Spirit said: set apart Barnabas and Saul. They fasted, prayed, laid hands on them, and sent them.

Niger.meaning: Simeon's Latin nickname, meaning dark or black

Manaen.meaning: a teacher brought up with Herod the tetrarch

tetrarch.meaning: a ruler of part of a kingdom

notes: Acts 13:2 paraphrased; the Douay-Rheims wording and name order (Saul and Barnabas / Barnabas and Saul) were not certain.
'Niger' as a Latin nickname for dark/black and Simeon possibly being African: common in commentaries but uncertain; the script says only 'likely an African or two'. Confirm.
Manaen 'brought up with' Herod Antipas (syntrophos: foster brother or courtier); confirm.
Greek aphorizō in Acts 13:2 and Romans 1:1: confirm form and pronunciation.
Catholic fasting norms in howItsDone (US practice): confirm.
